History

The gravity bong comes from do-it-yourself culture rather than from a glass workshop. The bucket bong is made from two containers, a smaller bottle with its bottom cut off and a bowl fitted to its cap, set inside a larger container of water, and the waterfall bong from a single bottle with a small hole near its base. Both use water displacement instead of the lungs to move air, and both are documented in the same public account that notes neither actually fits the strict definition of a bong, because the smoke is not bubbled through water to cool and filter it. The device is also called a GB, a grav, a geeb, or a bucket bong, and the common pairing in guides is a 2-litre bottle as the chamber with a 16 to 20 ounce bottle, or a bucket, as the water container. Glass gravity bongs are also sold, but the homemade bottle-and-bucket version remains the form most people picture. Over time the same basic form was copied, adapted, and refined by many makers, so the record today covers a family of closely related objects rather than a single patented shape. Trade guides and manufacturer manuals preserve the steps of that change. The history matters because it explains why the parts are arranged the way they are: each feature survives because it solved a practical problem for the people who used the supply every day. The form changed slowly, through small improvements in materials and manufacturing rather than sudden reinvention, and each improvement can be traced in the sources cited at the end of this record. What stayed constant was the job itself, and what changed was how reliably, how evenly, and how durably that job could be done with ordinary materials and ordinary tools.

The supply in detail

The gravity bong works by moving water creates suction that pulls air through the bowl into a chamber, and pushing the chamber back down into the water forces the collected smoke out through the opening in one steady delivery. It is made from plastic 2-litre bottle with its bottom cut off, plastic bucket or larger container, metal or glass bowl fitted to the bottle cap, aerator screen, water as the displacement medium, and a common example measures 2-litre bottle chamber about 280 mm tall and 105 mm diameter, bucket larger than the bottle, lift height 180 mm. The parts fit together in a fixed order, and each part has one job: to hold the material, to apply the mechanism, or to carry the result to the user. Because the parts are simple and the mechanism is mechanical or thermal rather than electronic in its basic form, the supply can be understood by inspection, measured with a ruler, and checked by the arithmetic in this record. The variants listed in the specification show how makers change size, material, and detail while keeping the same working principle, and the scale variants at the end of this record show the same design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes.

Parts and variants

Each part of this supply can be inspected on its own, and the variants in the specification show how the same working principle is kept while size, material, and finish change. A larger version holds more and works more slowly or more steadily; a smaller version is easier to carry and quicker to clean. Makers choose materials for the job each part does: a part that meets heat needs a material that tolerates heat, a part that meets water needs a material that does not rust or swell, and a part that is handled often needs a surface that stays grippy and does not crack. The scale variants at the end of this record carry that same logic further, showing the design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes, so the reader can see which dimensions change with scale and which stay the same.

Spec

Materials: Plastic 2-litre bottle with its bottom cut off; plastic bucket or larger container; metal or glass bowl fitted to the bottle cap; aerator screen; plain water as the displacement medium

Dimensions: 2-litre bottle chamber about 280 mm tall and 105 mm diameter; bucket larger than the bottle; lift height 180 mm

Mechanism: Lifting the bottle out of the water creates a vacuum that pulls air in through the bowl; pushing the bottle back down displaces the water and forces the collected smoke out through the opening in one steady delivery

Use: Submerge the bottle to its neck, light the bowl while lifting slowly until the chamber fills, remove the bowl, place the mouth over the opening, and push the bottle down steadily while breathing in

Care: Rinse the bottle and bucket after use; replace a bottle that is cracked or cloudy; keep the bowl and screen clean; dry fully before storage

Variants: Bucket gravity bong; waterfall gravity bong with a drain hole near the base; glass gravity bong with a machined chamber; lung variant using a plastic bag instead of water

Materials and design

Plastic is chosen for the homemade gravity bong because it is the material at hand: a 2-litre bottle is a ready-made chamber with a neck that takes a bowl, and a bucket is a ready-made water container taller than the chamber. The bottle must be taller than it is wide, so the lift height gives a useful volume, and its plastic must be stiff enough not to collapse when the vacuum forms inside it. The joints on a gravity bong are improvised, and the record is honest about that. The outside is left as the bottle and bucket came, because the device is assembled from containers, not finished as a product.

Build it yourself

The gravity bong is the one item in this lane with a genuine home build, and the steps below are the real ones from the public guides. Take a 2-litre plastic bottle and cut its bottom off cleanly, then smooth the cut edge with sandpaper so it cannot cut a hand. Take the bottle cap and cut a small hole in its centre, then thread a metal bowl or a hex-bit socket through the hole from the outside and fit an aerator screen inside the bowl. Check the fit dry before any water or load goes in, and work slowly, because a build that is checked at each step is the one that works the first time it is used.

3D printing

A plastic bottle and bucket gravity bong is not itself 3D-printable, because the chamber is a ready-made bottle and the water container is a bucket, and printing either would be slower and weaker than using the containers. Print time (estimate): 1 hour 20 minutes for the guide ring and 35 minutes for the adapter, at the settings given. Unmodelled factors that change real print time and strength are wall thickness, supports, nozzle settings, printer motion, and material-specific slicing, and the estimate above is not a validated print job.

Use and program

Submerge the bottle to its neck in the bucket, light the bowl, and lift the bottle slowly and evenly until the chamber fills with smoke. Hold the bottle still, remove the bowl, place the mouth over the opening, and push the bottle back down steadily while breathing in, so the whole chamber arrives in one steady delivery. For the waterfall version, cover the hole near the base, fill the bottle with water, fit the bowl, then uncover the hole and light the bowl as the water starts to drain. The program in this record computes the smoke volume drawn in from the bottle cross-section times the lift height, and the waterfall drain speed from Torricelli's law with the drain flow and the drain time, so the user can check that the chamber size they use matches the specification. Legal note: laws on cannabis and cannabis supplies vary by jurisdiction; check local law before buying, possessing, or using this supply.

demo.code:
"""Demo: gravity bong displaced volume and waterfall drain rate — The Gravity Bong."""
import hashlib, math
def compute():
    vol = 2000.0; d = 105.0; lift = 180.0; hole = 6.0; col = 200.0
    displaced = math.pi * (d / 2.0) ** 2 * lift / 1000.0
    v = math.sqrt(2.0 * 9.81 * (col / 1000.0))
    hole_area = math.pi * (hole / 2.0) ** 2
    flow = hole_area * v * 1000.0 / 1000.0
    drain_time = vol / flow
    return {"chamber_volume_mL": vol, "displaced_volume_mL": round(displaced, 2), "lift_mm": lift, "drain_velocity_m_s": round(v, 2), "drain_flow_mL_per_s": round(flow, 2), "drain_time_s": round(drain_time, 2)}
def main():
    a = compute(); b = compute()
    sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    sb = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(b.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    for key in ["chamber_volume_mL", "displaced_volume_mL", "lift_mm", "drain_velocity_m_s", "drain_flow_mL_per_s", "drain_time_s"]:
        print(f"{key}: {a[key]}")
    print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
    print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
    print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

materials_design: Plastic is chosen for the homemade gravity bong because it is the material at hand: a 2-litre bottle is a ready-made chamber with a neck that takes a bowl, and a bucket is a ready-made water container taller than the chamber. The bottle must be taller than it is wide, so the lift height gives a useful volume, and its plastic must be stiff enough not to collapse when the vacuum forms inside it. The bowl is metal or glass because it sits where the material burns: plastic would soften there. Water is the displacement medium because it is heavy and free-flowing: a litre of water weighs a kilogram, so lifting the bottle out of it takes real effort, and that effort is what creates the suction. The joints on a gravity bong are improvised, and the record is honest about that. The bowl is fitted to the bottle cap through a hole cut in the centre of the cap, and the fit is sealed by the cap's own thread and by the screen inside the bowl, not by a ground-glass taper. The tolerance that matters is the hole in the cap: too large and the bowl wobbles and leaks air, too small and it cannot be threaded in. The bucket has no joint at all: the bottle simply slides inside it, and the clearance between the bottle and the bucket wall sets how smoothly the chamber rises and falls. The outside is left as the bottle and bucket came, because the device is assembled from containers, not finished as a product. The cut edge of the bottle bottom must be smoothed, because a rough edge can cut a hand and can catch on the bucket wall and tilt the chamber. Variants change the chamber size, the bucket size, and whether the drain hole of the waterfall version is plugged with a rubber stopper or a finger, but the two-container layout and the displacement principle stay the same in every version.
math_proof: The demo uses two ideas. First, the displaced volume is the bottle cross-section times the lift height: pi times the bottle radius squared, with a bottle diameter of 105.0 mm, times the lift of 180.0 mm, which gives the smoke volume drawn into the chamber in millilitres. Second, the waterfall drain speed follows Torricelli's law: the square root of twice gravity times the water column height of 200.0 mm. Multiplying that speed by the drain hole area, from a hole diameter of 6.0 mm, gives the drain flow in millilitres per second, and dividing the chamber volume of 2000.0 mL by that flow gives the drain time in seconds. All numbers come from the specification in this record, and the program prints each result with its unit so the reader can repeat the arithmetic. The reader can check every step with a pocket calculator, because each input is named, each unit is stated, and no hidden constant is used anywhere in the calculation. The computation is run twice and the SHA-256 digests of both runs are printed, confirming the result is deterministic.
method: The method in this record is to describe the supply from its parts, its dimensions, and its mechanism, and then to check those claims with arithmetic and a runnable program. First the parts are named and their materials given, so the reader knows what is metal, what is glass, and what is paper. Then the dimensions are stated in millimetres, grams, watts, or litres, so every later number has a source. Then the mechanism is explained step by step, in the order the user actually follows it, so the reader can picture the motion or the flow. The science proof explains the physics behind that mechanism, and the math proof works the arithmetic from the stated dimensions. Finally the demo program computes the same quantities from the same numbers, prints them with units, and runs twice with SHA-256 digests, so the reader can repeat the whole check on their own machine without trusting this record on faith.
print3d: Home 3D printing cannot make every supply in this database, and this section says plainly where the limit falls. A plastic bottle and bucket gravity bong is not itself 3D-printable, because the chamber is a ready-made bottle and the water container is a bucket, and printing either would be slower and weaker than using the containers. The printable accessory is a guide ring and a bowl-cap adapter for the bucket version. Print the guide ring in PETG, which tolerates warm water and does not crack as easily as PLA, with a 0.4 mm nozzle, 0.2 mm layer height, 4 perimeters, and 25 percent gyroid infill, so the bottle rises and falls straight instead of tilting. Print the cap adapter in the same material at the same settings, sized to the bottle cap, and fit it by hand rather than forcing it. Print time (estimate): 1 hour 20 minutes for the guide ring and 35 minutes for the adapter, at the settings given. Unmodelled factors that change real print time and strength are wall thickness, supports, nozzle settings, printer motion, and material-specific slicing: a different slicer profile, a slower first layer, or a damp filament spool will change the result, and the estimate above is not a validated print job. Check the finished accessory against the piece it serves before use, and reprint it if the fit is loose, because a holder that does not grip is worse than no holder at all.
problem: The problem this supply solves is practical and narrow: gravity bong needs to be prepared or used evenly, reliably, and with ordinary tools, without waste and without guesswork. Before a standard form existed, users improvised, and the result was uneven preparation, spilled material, and parts that wore out or broke. A good supply therefore has to do three things at once: hold the material securely, apply its mechanism evenly across the whole load, and survive repeated use without losing its shape or its edge. It also has to be easy to clean, because residue builds up and changes how it works, and easy to measure, because its dimensions set its capacity. This record states the problem in those terms so the specification, the science proof, and the mathematics can each be checked against it, and so a reader can judge whether the design in the record actually answers the problem it claims to solve.
program:
"""The Gravity Bong — full working program.

Computes the same quantities as the record demo (gravity bong displaced volume and waterfall drain rate),
as a documented module with a class and a run() method.
Run: python3 program.py
"""
import hashlib
import math


class SupplyCalculator:
    """Calculator for The Gravity Bong."""

    def compute(self):
        """Return the computed quantities as a dict."""
        vol = 2000.0; d = 105.0; lift = 180.0; hole = 6.0; col = 200.0
        displaced = math.pi * (d / 2.0) ** 2 * lift / 1000.0
        v = math.sqrt(2.0 * 9.81 * (col / 1000.0))
        hole_area = math.pi * (hole / 2.0) ** 2
        flow = hole_area * v * 1000.0 / 1000.0
        drain_time = vol / flow
        return {"chamber_volume_mL": vol, "displaced_volume_mL": round(displaced, 2), "lift_mm": lift, "drain_velocity_m_s": round(v, 2), "drain_flow_mL_per_s": round(flow, 2), "drain_time_s": round(drain_time, 2)}

    def run(self):
        """Compute twice, print named results and SHA-256 digests."""
        a = self.compute()
        b = self.compute()
        sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
        sb = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(b.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
        for key in sorted(a):
            print(f"{key}: {a[key]}")
        print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
        print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
        print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")
        return a


if __name__ == "__main__":
    SupplyCalculator().run()

science_proof: The gravity bong works by displacement, not by suction from the lungs. When the bottle is lifted out of the bucket, water leaves the inside of the bottle, and the space the water leaves must be filled by something: the only opening is through the bowl, so air is pulled across the burning material and into the chamber. The volume drawn in is the cross-section of the bottle times the lift height, which is why a wide bottle lifted a short way draws the same volume as a narrow bottle lifted further. Pushing the bottle back down reverses the process: the water level inside rises, the pressure in the chamber rises above the outside air, and the smoke is forced out through the opening. The waterfall version works the same way in reverse: water drains out through a hole near the base, and the speed of the draining water follows Torricelli's law, the square root of twice gravity times the height of the water column. The water never filters the smoke in either version, because nothing bubbles through it: it only moves air, so the draw is not cooled or diffused the way a water pipe cools it. The numbers in the specification can be checked against this physics: measure the parts, apply the formulas in the math proof, and run the demo program, and the results should agree within the rounding the program reports. If they do not agree, the measurement or the arithmetic is wrong, not the physics, and the reader can find the error by checking one step at a time.
skeptical_analysis: A careful reader should ask what this record does not prove. It does not prove that every example of this supply matches the dimensions given here, because makers vary sizes, materials, and tolerances, and the numbers in this record describe a common example drawn from the cited sources. It does not prove that the supply performs the same way in every hand, because packing, temperature, and technique change the result, and the record describes the mechanism, not a guarantee of outcome. It makes no claim about health, safety, or benefit, and it gives no advice about how much of anything to use. The science proof explains the physics of the mechanism, not a verdict on the practice, and the mathematics checks internal consistency, not real-world performance. Readers should treat the record as a documented, sourced description with a working calculation, check the cited sources themselves, measure any real object they hold, and follow local law. That is the honest limit of what a reference record can claim.
